--- title: "PowSyBl & Dynawo" subtitle: "Part 1 · What they are and why GridFM uses them" description: "Two open-source simulators built for transmission system operators, and the role each one plays in GridFM-Datakit." jupyter: python3 --- ::: {.session-strip} [15 min]{.chip} [Part 1 of 4]{.chip} [pypowsybl · pypowsybl.dynamic]{.chip} ::: ::: {.goals} #### In this part - Place PowSyBl and Dynawo in the GridFM-Datakit pipeline. - Load a grid, solve a power flow and draw it with pypowsybl. - Move a grid between exchange formats and see what each one keeps. - Run a first Dynawo time-domain simulation from Python and plot it. ::: ## Two tools from the control room Both projects started at RTE, the French transmission system operator, and are developed in the open. Operators use them for real operational and planning studies, which is what makes them interesting as a source of training data. | | **PowSyBl** | **Dynawo** | |---|---|---| | What | Framework to model, exchange and simulate grids | Time-domain simulator, RMS (phasor) | | Core | Java, with the Python binding **pypowsybl** | C++ solver, Modelica models compiled ahead of time | | Grid formats | CGMES, UCTE, PSS/E, XIIDM, MATPOWER | Reads the grid from PowSyBl | | Simulations | Load flow (OpenLoadFlow), security analysis, sensitivities, short circuit, remedial action optimizer | Short-term stability (DynaSwing), long-term stability (DynaWaltz), steady state with automata (DynaFlow) | | Home | [powsybl.org](https://www.powsybl.org), an LF Energy project | [dynawo.github.io](https://dynawo.github.io) | ::: {.center} ![](../assets/logos/powsybl-logo.png){width=180}     ![](../assets/logos/dynawo-logo.png){width=150}     ![](../assets/logos/lf-energy-logo.png){width=150} ::: ## Why GridFM-Datakit integrates them A foundation model learns what its data shows it. Datakit already produced large steady-state datasets from MATPOWER cases with PowerModels.jl. PowSyBl and Dynawo extend it in three directions. 1. **Industrial grids in.** PowSyBl reads the formats operators exchange every day, so a dataset can start from a realistic network instead of a textbook case. 2. **Industrial-grade physics out.** OpenLoadFlow and Dynawo are the solvers used on real operational studies, which narrows the gap between synthetic data and the field. 3. **Time as a new modality.** Dynawo turns each operating point into a trajectory, and randomized disturbances become a new axis of data augmentation. ![The datakit pipeline. PowSyBl reads the grid and solves the power flow, Dynawo simulates the time domain.](../assets/pipeline.png){width=800 fig-alt="Pipeline from grid model through PowSyBl, datakit perturbation, OPF, topology outages and power flow, to a steady-state dataset and through Dynawo to trajectories."} ::: {.callout-note title="The same identifiers everywhere"} Every element keeps the ID it has in the network file, from the PowSyBl network to the Dynawo model mapping and the output tables. That is what lets a configuration file say "disconnect `_GEN____2_SM` at 1 s". ::: ## PowSyBl in a few lines The IEEE 14-bus case used throughout the dynamic parts ships as an XIIDM file, the native PowSyBl format. ::: {#ab6275b2 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd import pypowsybl as pp network = pp.network.load("../data/ieee14/IEEE14.iidm") network.get_generators()[ ["name", "target_p", "target_v", "max_p", "voltage_regulator_on"] ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
name target_p target_v max_p voltage_regulator_on
id
_GEN____1_SM GEN    1 232.3463 73.140 9999.0 True
_GEN____2_SM GEN    2 40.0000 72.105 9999.0 True
_GEN____3_SM GEN    3 0.0000 69.690 9999.0 True
_GEN____6_SM GEN    6 0.0000 14.766 9999.0 True
_GEN____8_SM GEN    8 0.0000 15.042 9999.0 True
``` ::: ::: Every element type is a pandas DataFrame, and every attribute can be updated in place. A load flow with OpenLoadFlow fills in the voltages and the flows. ::: {#239f8ca1 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} result = pp.loadflow.run_ac(network) print(result[0].status_text, "in", result[0].iteration_count, "iterations") network.get_buses()[["v_mag", "v_angle"]].round(2).head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Converged in 3 iterations ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
v_mag v_angle
id
_BUS___10_VL_0 14.50 -4.78
_BUS___11_VL_0 14.59 -4.48
_BUS___12_VL_0 14.56 -4.76
_BUS___13_VL_0 14.50 -4.84
_BUS___14_VL_0 14.29 -5.72
``` ::: ::: PowSyBl models equipment in detail, and OpenLoadFlow can control it. On a copy of the grid, the ratio tap changer of the transformer between buses 4 and 9 starts at its lowest tap and regulates the voltage of bus 9 to 14.3 kV. ::: {#1fc4536b .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} regulated = pp.network.load("../data/ieee14/IEEE14.iidm") transformer = "_BUS____4-BUS____9-1_PT" regulated.update_ratio_tap_changers( id=transformer, tap=1, oltc=True, regulated_side="TWO", target_v=14.3, target_deadband=0.1, ) regulated.update_ratio_tap_changers(id=transformer, regulating=True) result = pp.loadflow.run_ac( regulated, pp.loadflow.Parameters(transformer_voltage_control_on=True) ) print(result[0].status_text, "in", result[0].iteration_count, "iterations") tap = regulated.get_ratio_tap_changers().loc[transformer] print("tap", tap.tap, "solved at", tap.solved_tap_position) pd.DataFrame( {"base case": network.get_buses().v_mag, "regulated": regulated.get_buses().v_mag} ).loc[["_BUS____9_VL_0"]].round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Converged in 9 iterations tap 1 solved at 10 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
base case regulated
id
_BUS____9_VL_0 14.57 14.31
``` ::: ::: The load flow leaves `tap` at its set value and reports the position it chose in `solved_tap_position`. The base case `network` is untouched, so the rest of this part runs on the original grid. PowSyBl also draws the grid. The network explorer of pypowsybl-jupyter shows the network area diagram around a voltage level, with its flows, and the single line diagram of that voltage level. Pick another voltage level, or raise the depth to see more of the grid. The voltage levels keep the place they have in a diagram of the whole grid, passed as `fixed_nad_positions`, so the drawing grows around them instead of being laid out again at each depth. ::: {#37ae0ed9 .cell .column-page-left execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} import json from pypowsybl_jupyter import network_explorer layout = json.loads(network.get_network_area_diagram().metadata) positions = pd.DataFrame(layout["nodes"]).set_index("equipmentId")[["x", "y"]] network_explorer(network, fixed_nad_positions=positions.rename_axis("id")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Exchange formats European operators exchange grid models as **CGMES**, the Common Grid Model Exchange Standard. PowSyBl writes and reads it, as well as its own **XIIDM** format. A round trip shows what each one keeps. It runs on the PEGASE 89-bus case of PGLib, the grid of Part 2, which GridFM-Datakit's PowSyBl reader turns from a MATPOWER file into a pypowsybl network. ::: {#05a004d6 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} from pathlib import Path from gridfm_datakit.network import get_pglib_source_path from gridfm_datakit.powsybl import load_net Path("outputs/part1").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) grid = load_net(get_pglib_source_path("case89_pegase")).pp_net grid.save("outputs/part1/pegase89.zip", format="CGMES") grid.save( "outputs/part1/pegase89_cgmes3.zip", format="CGMES", parameters={"iidm.export.cgmes.cim-version": "100"}, ) grid.save("outputs/part1/pegase89.xiidm", format="XIIDM") copies = { "MATPOWER source": grid, "CGMES 2.4.15": pp.network.load("outputs/part1/pegase89.zip"), "CGMES 3": pp.network.load("outputs/part1/pegase89_cgmes3.zip"), "XIIDM": pp.network.load("outputs/part1/pegase89.xiidm"), } pd.DataFrame( { name: [ len(n.get_buses()), len(n.get_generators()), len(n.get_branches()), len(n.get_loading_limits()), ] for name, n in copies.items() }, index=["buses", "generators", "branches", "loading limits"], ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
MATPOWER source CGMES 2.4.15 CGMES 3 XIIDM
buses 89 89 87 89
generators 12 12 12 12
branches 210 210 210 210
loading limits 1260 0 1260 1260
``` ::: ::: A MATPOWER case rates its branches in apparent power. CGMES 2.4.15 holds apparent power limits in its Equipment Operation profile, which PowSyBl does not write for a bus-branch model like this one, so they are lost. CGMES 3 moved them into the core equipment profile and keeps them, but two buses go missing on the way back. XIIDM keeps everything, so that is the file GridFM-Datakit gets in Part 2. A CGMES file from an operator, whose limits are currents, goes in the same way. ## A first Dynawo simulation `pypowsybl.dynamic` drives Dynawo with three mappings. **Models** attach a dynamic model to a static element, **events** say what happens and when, and **output variables** say what to record. The physical parameters of each model come from a `.par` file, referenced by a parameter set ID. ::: {#5a42e198 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pypowsybl.dynamic as dyn models_table = pd.read_csv("../data/ieee14/static_element_dynamic_models.csv") machines = models_table.query("category_name == 'SynchronousGenerator'") machines ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
category_name static_id parameter_set_id model_name
0 SynchronousGenerator _GEN____1_SM Generator1 GeneratorSynchronousFourWindingsProportionalRe...
1 SynchronousGenerator _GEN____2_SM Generator2 GeneratorSynchronousFourWindingsProportionalRe...
2 SynchronousGenerator _GEN____3_SM Generator3 GeneratorSynchronousFourWindingsProportionalRe...
3 SynchronousGenerator _GEN____6_SM Generator6 GeneratorSynchronousThreeWindingsProportionalR...
4 SynchronousGenerator _GEN____8_SM Generator8 GeneratorSynchronousThreeWindingsProportionalR...
``` ::: ::: The five machines get a synchronous generator model. Loads and other elements keep Dynawo's default model. ::: {#69300791 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} models = dyn.ModelMapping() for row in machines.itertuples(): models.add_synchronous_generator( static_id=row.static_id, parameter_set_id=row.parameter_set_id, model_name=row.model_name, ) ``` ::: The disturbance is a 100 ms solid fault on bus 4, cleared without tripping anything. ::: {#55542ab9 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} events = dyn.EventMapping() events.add_node_fault( static_id="_BUS____4_TN", start_time=1.0, fault_time=0.1, r_pu=0.0, x_pu=0.01 ) outputs = dyn.OutputVariableMapping() outputs.add_standard_model_curves(static_id="_BUS____4_TN", variables=["U_value"]) for gen in machines.static_id: outputs.add_dynamic_model_curves( dynamic_model_id=gen, variables=["generator_omegaPu_value"] ) ``` ::: The solver settings live in the same `.par` file. `IDAOrder2` is a variable-step solver, fine enough to follow a fault. ::: {#f37b57a8 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} par = "../data/ieee14/IEEE14.par" parameters = dyn.Parameters( start_time=0.0, stop_time=10.0, provider_parameters={ "parametersFile": par, "network.parametersFile": par, "network.parametersId": "Network", "solver.type": "IDA", "solver.parametersFile": par, "solver.parametersId": "IDAOrder2", }, ) simulation = dyn.Simulation() result = simulation.run(network, models, events, outputs, parameters) print(result.status()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` DynamicSimulationStatus.SUCCESS ``` ::: ::: The curves come back as one DataFrame indexed by time. ::: {#736cb500 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} curves = result.curves() curves.index = (curves.index - curves.index[0]).total_seconds() fig, (ax_u, ax_w) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4)) ax_u.plot(curves.index, curves["NETWORK__BUS____4_TN_U_value"], color=PALETTE[0]) ax_u.set(title="Voltage at bus 4", xlabel="time (s)", ylabel="kV") for i, gen in enumerate(machines.static_id): ax_w.plot( curves.index, curves[f"{gen}_generator_omegaPu_value"], color=PALETTE[i], label=gen.strip("_").replace("____", " ").replace("_SM", ""), ) ax_w.set(title="Rotor speed", xlabel="time (s)", ylabel="pu") ax_w.legend(ncols=2) fig.tight_layout() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](01-powsybl-dynawo_files/figure-html/cell-13-output-1.png){width=1199 height=429} ::: ::: The fault collapses the voltage at bus 4, and the rotor speeds of the machines swing, then settle. This is one trajectory. Parts 3 and 4 produce thousands of them, each from a different operating point and a different disturbance. ## Your turn ::: {.callout-tip .exercise title="Exercise · Trip a generator"} Replace the fault by the disconnection of generator 2 at 1 s with `events.add_disconnection(static_id=..., start_time=...)`. Run the simulation for 30 s and plot the rotor speed of generator 1. How does the response differ from the fault? ::: ::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Show a solution"} ::: {#3549c9d3 .cell tags='["solution"]' execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} network = pp.network.load("../data/ieee14/IEEE14.iidm") pp.loadflow.run_ac(network) trip = dyn.EventMapping() trip.add_disconnection(static_id="_GEN____2_SM", start_time=1.0) parameters = dyn.Parameters( start_time=0.0, stop_time=30.0, provider_parameters=parameters.provider_parameters, ) result = simulation.run(network, models, trip, outputs, parameters) curves = result.curves() curves.index = (curves.index - curves.index[0]).total_seconds() ax = curves["_GEN____1_SM_generator_omegaPu_value"].plot(color=PALETTE[0]) ax.set( title="Rotor speed of generator 1 after tripping generator 2", xlabel="time (s)", ylabel="pu", ); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](01-powsybl-dynawo_files/figure-html/cell-14-output-1.png){width=870 height=429} ::: ::: Losing a machine is a lasting power imbalance. The speed drops and settles at a new value set by the governors, where a cleared fault leaves the system where it started. ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Next"} [Part 2](02-steady-state.qmd) feeds the PEGASE grid through PowSyBl into datakit and builds a steady-state dataset. :::
